questions.q: What are the four steps of the portfolio-sort recipe used to build factors like SMB and HML?
options: Download the factor from a data vendor, verify it, publish it, rebalance it
Rank stocks by a characteristic, bucket them, go long one bucket and short another, hold until the next rebalance
Run a time-series regression, extract residuals, square them, average them
Cluster stocks with k-means, pick the two largest clusters, merge them
questions.explain: Every Fama-French-style factor is built by ranking stocks on a characteristic, splitting into buckets, and going long one bucket / short the other until the next rebalancing date.

questions.q: Why does the momentum factor rank stocks on the 12-1 month return rather than the full prior 12-month return?
options: Data for the most recent month is usually unavailable
The most recent month is excluded to avoid short-term reversal, which would contaminate a pure momentum signal
12-1 month returns are easier to annualize
Regulators require excluding the most recent month
questions.explain: The most recent month is skipped because of well-documented short-term reversal in stock returns, which would otherwise contaminate the momentum signal.

questions.q: What is look-ahead bias in the context of building a value factor like HML?
options: Using too few stocks in the universe
Using fundamental data (like book value) on a date before it was actually publicly reported
Rebalancing too frequently
Using data from international markets
questions.explain: Fundamental data like book value is reported with a lag; using it on the fiscal-year-end date itself (before it was publicly available) is look-ahead bias, which real implementations avoid by lagging fundamentals by several months.

questions.q: In the worked example, how did average next-month return vary across the three book-to-market buckets (low/growth, mid, high/value)?
options: It was identical across all three buckets
It decreased monotonically from growth to value
The low (growth) bucket was lowest at 0.0098, the mid bucket highest at 0.0204, and the high (value) bucket in between at 0.0194 -- not perfectly monotonic, which real factor sorts often show too
The high (value) bucket had negative returns
questions.explain: The guide's worked example shows growth lowest (0.0098), mid highest (0.0204), and value in between (0.0194) -- a reminder that real-world sorts don't always produce a perfectly clean monotonic pattern across buckets.

questions.q: Why is momentum considered one of the more expensive factors to actually trade, despite looking attractive on paper?
options: It requires options rather than stocks
It has high turnover -- last month's winners are frequently not this month's winners, requiring frequent rebalancing
It is illegal to trade in most markets
It only works on bonds, which have high trading costs
questions.explain: Momentum's signal decays quickly, leading to high turnover and correspondingly high transaction costs once realistic trading costs are factored in.
